lessonTitle: Creep Behaviour: Stages, Power Law and Arrhenius Dependence

blocks.text: A superheater tube in a coal-fired boiler runs at 550 °C and about 60 MPa hoop stress for twenty years. It is never overloaded, but each year its diameter grows by a fraction of a percent until a bulge appears and the tube ruptures. Metals deform slowly under steady load when they are hot, and the rate depends sharply on both stress and temperature.

blocks.markdown: **Creep** is time-dependent plastic deformation under constant stress. It becomes significant above roughly $0.4$ of the absolute melting temperature $T_m$ (about 0.3 to 0.4 in some alloys). A creep test holds a specimen at constant load and temperature and records strain against time. The curve has three stages and ends in rupture.

rows: Nearly straight line; most of the life
Necking, cavity formation, grain boundary sliding, microstructure degradation
blocks.caption: The minimum (secondary) creep rate is the main design parameter.

blocks.title: Minimum creep rate
blocks.text: The minimum creep rate $\dot\varepsilon_s$ is the slope of the strain-time curve in stage II (units 1/s or %/h). It is the quantity used to estimate how fast a component deforms in service.

blocks.caption: Norton's power law at fixed temperature. $\sigma$ is the stress (MPa); $B$ and $n$ are constants of the material and temperature; $n$ is typically 3 to 8 for metals in the dislocation creep regime.

blocks.markdown: Creep is thermally activated: atoms and dislocations need thermal energy to climb or diffuse. This gives an **Arrhenius** temperature dependence, in which the rate depends on $\exp(-Q/RT)$. Combining it with Norton's law gives the standard form.

blocks.caption: $Q$ = activation energy for creep (J/mol), $R=8.314$ J/(mol K), $T$ = absolute temperature (K), $A$ = material constant.

blocks.title: Minimum creep rate at a given stress and temperature
blocks.prompt: A material has (assumed) $A=0.1$ s$^{-1}$MPa$^{-5}$, $n=5$ and $Q=300$ kJ/mol. Find $\dot\varepsilon_s$ at $\sigma = 80$ MPa and $T = 550\,^\circ$C.

steps.text: Convert to percent per 1000 h: multiply by $3.6\times10^{6}$ s per 1000 h, and by 100 percent.

blocks.answer: About 2.98\times10^{-11} per second, i.e. 0.0107 percent per 1000 h.

blocks.title: The effect of temperature and stress
blocks.prompt: For the same material, (a) by what factor does the rate increase when the temperature is raised from 800 K to 850 K at constant stress? (b) by what factor when the stress is doubled at constant temperature?

steps.text: Both factors are greater than one: hotter or more heavily loaded material creeps faster.

blocks.answer: A 50 K rise multiplies the rate about 14.2 times; doubling the stress multiplies it 32 times.

blocks.title: Finding Q from data
blocks.text: Taking logarithms, $\ln\dot\varepsilon_s=\ln(A\sigma^n)-Q/(RT)$. A plot of $\ln\dot\varepsilon_s$ against $1/T$ at fixed stress is a straight line of slope $-Q/R$; a plot of $\ln\dot\varepsilon_s$ against $\ln\sigma$ at fixed temperature has slope $n$.

items: Primary creep is brief; secondary creep sets the rate used in design; tertiary creep signals imminent rupture.
Doubling the stress raises the rate by $2^n$; with $n=5$ that is a factor of 32.
A small temperature rise raises the rate by a large factor because of the exponential, which is why metal temperature control matters.

blocks.title: Absolute temperature
blocks.text: Always use kelvin in the exponential. Using degrees Celsius gives meaningless results, because the exponent depends on $1/T$ with $T$ measured from absolute zero.

points: The creep curve has primary (decreasing rate), secondary (constant minimum rate) and tertiary (accelerating) stages.
$\dot\varepsilon_s=B\sigma^n$ at fixed temperature (Norton), and $\dot\varepsilon_s=A\sigma^n e^{-Q/RT}$ in general.
The Arrhenius dependence makes creep extremely sensitive to temperature; use kelvin and ratios to compare conditions.

questions.stem: Which stage of the creep curve shows an approximately constant strain rate and takes most of the life?

distractorRationale.d: Elastic loading is not part of creep strain.

questions.explanation: In stage II work hardening is balanced by thermal recovery, so the strain rate is constant at its minimum. This stage usually occupies most of the time to rupture.

questions.stem: What happens to the strain rate in tertiary creep?

options.text: It increases until rupture, due to necking and internal cavities

questions.correctOptionText: It increases until rupture, due to necking and internal cavities

distractorRationale.a: Rates fall in primary creep, not tertiary.

questions.explanation: In stage III the effective section reduces by necking and cavitation, raising the stress and accelerating the strain rate. The stage ends in rupture.

questions.stem: A component's metal temperature rises by 30 K with the stress unchanged. What is the effect on the minimum creep rate?

options.text: It rises by a large factor, following an Arrhenius dependence
It falls because the metal softens

questions.correctOptionText: It rises by a large factor, following an Arrhenius dependence

distractorRationale.b: The dependence is exponential, not linear.

questions.explanation: Creep is thermally activated, so the rate contains $\exp(-Q/RT)$. A modest rise in $T$ changes the exponent considerably and multiplies the rate by a large factor.

questions.stem: A material obeys $\dot\varepsilon_s\propto\sigma^{4}$. If the stress is doubled at the same temperature, by what factor does the minimum creep rate increase?
questions.explanation: With Norton's law $\dot\varepsilon_s\propto\sigma^n$, doubling $\sigma$ multiplies the rate by $2^n$. For $n=4$ this is a factor of 16.

questions.stem: On a plot of $\ln\dot\varepsilon_s$ against $1/T$ at constant stress, what does the slope represent?

options.text: $-Q/R$, the activation energy divided by the gas constant

questions.correctOptionText: $-Q/R$, the activation energy divided by the gas constant

distractorRationale.c: Melting temperature is unrelated to the slope.
distractorRationale.d: Rupture life is a separate quantity.

questions.explanation: Taking logs of the Arrhenius term gives a straight line in $1/T$ with slope $-Q/R$. This allows $Q$ to be found from measured rates at different temperatures.

questions.stem: A steel at a fixed temperature follows $\dot\varepsilon_s=B\sigma^n$ with $B=1\times10^{-18}$ s$^{-1}$MPa$^{-4}$ and $n=4$ (assumed). Find the minimum creep rate at $\sigma=150$ MPa in percent per 1000 h. (1000 h $=3.6\times10^{6}$ s.)
questions.explanation: $150^4=5.062\times10^{8}$, so $\dot\varepsilon_s=10^{-18}\times5.062\times10^{8}=5.06\times10^{-10}$ s$^{-1}$. Multiplying by $3.6\times10^{6}$ s and by 100 percent gives 0.182 percent per 1000 h.

questions.stem: A creep-resistant steel has $Q=250$ kJ/mol. By what factor does the minimum creep rate increase when the temperature rises from 700 K to 750 K at constant stress? Use $R = 8.314$ J/(mol K).
questions.explanation: The ratio is $\exp[(Q/R)(1/700-1/750)]=\exp[30072\times9.524\times10^{-5}]=\exp(2.864)=17.5$. A 50 K rise therefore multiplies the rate by about 18.

questions.stem: A material has $n=5$ and $Q=280$ kJ/mol. At 60 MPa and 800 K it creeps at a certain rate. Find the factor by which the rate increases at 75 MPa and 830 K. Use $R = 8.314$ J/(mol K).
questions.explanation: Stress factor: $(75/60)^5=3.052$. Temperature factor: $\exp[(280000/8.314)(1/800-1/830)]=4.58$. The product is 14, because the two effects multiply.

questions.stem: Sketch in words the strain-time curve of a constant-load creep test and explain the physical origin of the three stages.
markingGuide: Instantaneous elastic strain on loading, followed by the three stages
Primary: strain rate decreases as work hardening exceeds recovery
Secondary: constant minimum rate as hardening and thermal recovery balance; most of the life
Tertiary: rate increases due to necking, cavitation and microstructural damage, ending in rupture
States that the minimum creep rate is the design parameter
questions.explanation: The shape follows the competition between hardening and recovery, plus damage late in life. The constant secondary rate is the quantity used in design.

questions.stem: Creep rates measured at constant stress are $2.0\times10^{-9}$ s$^{-1}$ at 750 K and $3.5\times10^{-8}$ s$^{-1}$ at 800 K. (a) Determine the activation energy $Q$. (b) Predict the rate at 850 K at the same stress. State the assumption involved.
markingGuide: Predicts the 850 K rate by the same Arrhenius law as about 4.37\times10^{-7} s$^{-1}$
States the assumption that the same mechanism and $Q$ apply across the range (power-law creep), and that the temperatures are in kelvin
questions.explanation: Taking the ratio of the two rates removes $A\sigma^n$ and leaves $Q=R\ln(r_2/r_1)/(1/T_1-1/T_2)\approx286$ kJ/mol. Extrapolating to 850 K with this activation energy gives about 4.37\times10^{-7} s$^{-1}$, assuming the same creep mechanism.
